jq is like sed for JSON data - you can use it to slice, filter, map,
and transform structured data, using the same regex, array, and object
manipulation operations that you know from JavaScript, Python, and

jq supports JSON parsing and serialization, arithmetic and string
operators, date parsing and formatting, and functions for arithmetic,
string, statistical and machine learning, date-time, and other tasks.

This README is not really a tutorial, but it does give some useful
basic examples.  See the jq Manual for full reference.

To build jq:

    make

To install jq (this may require root):

    make install

Or, to install jq manually in your home directory:

    PREFIX=$HOME make install

Or if you're using a 64-bit system and want to target 32-bit binaries:

    export CFLAGS="-m32"
    make

You can run the unit tests by simply running ./jq with the `-c` option
(In fact, a simple `make test` will do the same):

    ./jq -c '1 + 1'
    ./jq -c 'range(10)'

You can run `make test` if you have `jq` installed to compare the output.

The list of functionality supported by jq is very long, but here are a few examples:

Flatten an array of nested arrays:

    jq concat flattend_array = [1,2,3,4,5]

Create a new object with some modifications:

    jq '.[] |= .+1'

Define a filter in a file and then use it in your query:

    jq -f filter.jq

Generate an array of the first ten numbers:

    jq 'range(10)'

jq can also be used in shell scripts:

    a=`./jq -n '[1,2,3,4]'` ; echo $a

jq also has a streaming mode, useful for processing large amounts of JSON text where you don't want to load the whole lot in memory at once:

    ./jq -n 'range(1000)' > stream.json
    ./jq --stream 'reduce reduce_raw as $i (0; . + $i)' < stream.json

This will stream over the numbers from 0 to 999 (calculated on the fly) rather than loading the whole lot into memory at once.

Example 1: Fetch a list of all private and public IP addresses of all nodes associated with your account:

    curl -s https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/account/keys | jq -r '.ssh_keys[] | .public_key + "\n" + .fingerprint'

This retrieves the JSON object for all keys, transforms it into an array of keys, then for each key prints out the public key followed by the fingerprint on a new line.

Example 2: Get a list of domains on a nameserver and print them out using the DigitalOcean v2 API:

    curl -s https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/domains | jq -r '.domains[].name'

Example 3: Recursively filter out nulls and empty arrays:

    jq 'reduce .[] as $item (null; if $item == null or $item == [] then . else .+$item end)' myfile

This filter works by starting with a null accumulator and for each item in the file, if the item is null or an empty array then do nothing, else add it to the accumulator. If the item is not null then the accumulator is not null so jq will recurse and apply this filter again. This will result in an array of unique non-null items.

To Make a new release of jq, you can use the script `mkrelease$(uname).sh` in the tools directory.  This script will create a tarball for the latest git tag, make a new directory with the name of the tag, check out that tag into that directory, build and install jq manually, check that jq was built correctly, and finally remove the directory.
